intro: “Some” and “any” talk about a quantity that is not exact. The basic rule is simple (some in positive sentences, any in negatives and questions), but you also need the exceptions for offers and polite requests.
objectifs: Use some in positive sentences and any in negative sentences and questions.
Choose between a / an and some, depending on whether the noun is singular, plural or uncountable.
Use some in questions to offer or ask for something (Would you like some tea?).
Use some and any alone, as pronouns (I haven't got any).

texte: Use “some” and “any” before a plural countable noun (eggs, apples) or an uncountable noun (milk, money). They show a quantity that we don't say exactly.
Use “some” in positive sentences, and “any” in negative sentences and questions.
exemples: I've got some friends in Montreal.

sections.titre: A / an or some? And when do we use nothing?
texte: With a singular countable noun, use “a” or “an”: “an apple”, “a banana”. “Some” and “any” are for plurals and uncountable nouns: “some apples”, “some water”.
When you talk about something in general, use no word: “I like coffee” (coffee in general). When you talk about an amount, use “some”: “I'd like some coffee” (a cup, a quantity).
“Some” is not always necessary: “We need eggs” and “We need some eggs” are both correct.

lignes: a / an: I haven't got an egg.

exemples: There's an orange and some grapes on the table.
I love chocolate. Can I have some?
General: no word. An amount: some.

texte: When you offer something or make a polite request, use “some” even in a question, because you expect the answer “yes”.
Compare: “Is there any coffee?” (a real question: is there coffee or not?) and “Would you like some coffee?” (an offer).
exemples: Can I have some water, please?
Could you give me some information about the course?
sections.note: “Any” in a positive sentence has another meaning: “it doesn't matter which”. “Take any seat” = sit where you want.

texte: You can replace “not … any” with “no” + noun and a positive verb: “There isn't any milk” = “There's no milk”. “No” is a little stronger.
Never use two negatives: “I haven't got no money” is wrong in standard English. Say “I haven't got any money” or “I've got no money”.
exemples: There aren't any buses on Sunday. = There are no buses on Sunday.
Two ways to say the same thing.

texte: When we already know the noun, we can use “some” and “any” alone: “I need eggs. Have you got any? — Yes, I've got some.”
Careful: don't put “of” between some / any and a noun: “some bread”, not “some of bread”. Use “some of” only before the, my, these…: “some of my friends”.
Words like something, anything, someone, nobody follow the same logic: see lesson 60.
exemples: I want some cake. Is there any left? — Sorry, there isn't any.
Some of my friends speak Spanish.

formule: some + plural / uncountable (positive, offers, requests) · any + plural / uncountable (negatives, questions)
prononciation: Before a noun, “some” is weak: “some water” = /səm ˈwɔːtə/. Alone or at the end of a sentence, it is strong: “Yes, I've got some” = /sʌm/.
Link before a vowel: “any eggs” = /ˌeni ˈeɡz/; “some apples” = /səm ˈæplz/.
In an offer, the voice goes up at the end: “Would you like some TEA? ↗”.
erreurs: Question: change the order and use “any”.
I'd like some water. / I'd like a glass of water.
I don't have any time. / I have no time.
There are some apples. / There aren't any apples.
Don't use “any” like this in a positive sentence.
Can I have any water, please?
Can I have some water, please?
I've got a friends in Brussels.
I've got some friends in Brussels.

dialogue.contexte: In Liège, Thomas and his flatmate Aminata want to make pancakes for some friends.
lignes: Let's make pancakes! Have we got any flour?
Yes, there's some flour in the cupboard.
Great. And are there any eggs?
Hmm, no, there aren't any eggs. And there's no milk.
OK, let's write a shopping list: eggs, milk and some sugar.
We've got some sugar. But we haven't got any butter.
Right: eggs, milk, butter. Do we need any juice for our friends?
Yes, let's get some orange juice. And would you like some coffee before we go?

exercices.consigne: Complete with a, an or some.
Write the sentence in the form given.
items: There isn't any milk. / There's no milk.
I haven't got any money. / I've got no money.
Has she got any friends here?

exercices.consigne: Each sentence has one mistake. Write it correctly.
items: There isn't any butter. / There's no butter.
Would you like any coffee? (an offer)
I need some flour. / I need flour.
I haven't got any. / I've got none.

exercices.consigne: Look at (or imagine) your fridge. Write four sentences: two things that are there (some) and two things that are not there (any). Then write your shopping list.
items: There's some cheese and there are some tomatoes. There isn't any milk and there aren't any eggs. Shopping list: milk, eggs, some bread and some fruit.

a_retenir: some + plural or uncountable in positive sentences; any in negatives and questions.
a / an before a singular countable noun; no word when you talk in general (I like coffee).
Offers and requests: some in the question (Would you like some tea? Can I have some water?).
not any = no; never two negatives (I haven't got any money / I've got no money).
some and any can stand alone (Have you got any? — Yes, I've got some).
